nodes.title: A1. Piece Rate (Lazear 2000, Safelite)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Layer output-contingent slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = \alpha + \beta\, s_i, \quad s_i = g(e_i) + \varepsilon_i$$

Worker's problem (CARA-Gaussian):
$$\max_{e_i}\; \alpha + \beta g(e_i) - c(e_i) - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\beta^2\sigma^2$$

FOC: $\beta\, g'(e_i^{*}) = c'(e_i^{*}) \Rightarrow e_i^{*} > 0$.

Optimal slope (Holmström–Milgrom 1987):
$$\beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\,\sigma^2\, k/g'^{\,2}}$$

Efficiency loss vs first-best: $\Delta = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\sigma^2(\beta^{*})^2$.

---

**Signal**: individual measured output.

**Solves**
- Connects worker utility to firm output.
- Strong effort incentive.
- Sorts high-productivity types into the firm (Safelite: ~half the 44% gain is sorting).

**Breaks**
- Measurement error → risk transfer.
- Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991).
- Ratchet (Gibbons 1987).
- Goodhart / bunching.
- Cooperation collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003).

**Use when**: output perfectly measurable, quality clearly enforceable, production individual (Safelite is the textbook case).

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study, 44% productivity gain).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (optimal linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. (1979)**. Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10, 74–91 (canonical PA setup).
- **Grossman, S. & Hart, O. (1983)**. An analysis of the principal-agent problem. *Econometrica*, 51(1), 7–45.
- **Mirrlees, J. (1975)**. The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. Working paper (later 1999 REStud).
- **Ross, S. (1973)**. The economic theory of agency: the principal's problem. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 63(2), 134–139.

nodes.title: A2. Tournament / Rank-Order Contest (Lazear–Rosen 1981)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Replace flat $w_0$ with rank-based prizes: winner gets $w_H$, loser $w_L$, spread $\Delta = w_H - w_L$. $P_i(\text{win})$ depends on relative effort.

Worker's problem:
$$\max_{e_i}\; \Delta \cdot P_i(\text{win} \mid e_i, e_{-i}) - c(e_i)$$

Lazear–Rosen (1981) optimal spread:
$$\Delta^{*} \cdot \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial e_i} = c'(e_i^{*})$$

Common noise $\varepsilon$ cancels — only *relative* effort determines rank.

---

**Signal**: your *rank* among peers, not your level.

**Solves**
- Cancels common shocks (market, weather, task difficulty) via relative comparison → attacks F1 (measurement).
- Fights the ratchet (F3): can't hide capacity if effort still moves rank.
- Simple prize structure; only ordinal ranking needed.

**Breaks**
- Sabotage (Chan 1996; Dye 1984; Lazear 1989).
- Collusion: everyone agrees to low effort.
- Kills cooperation completely — helping a peer is directly costly (worsens F5).
- Discourages risky innovation late in the round if ahead.

**Use when**: individual output measurable up to a common shock, peer group homogeneous, cooperation not required.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. & Rosen, S. (1981)**. Rank-order tournaments as optimum labor contracts. *JPE*, 89(5), 841–864.
- **Green, J. & Stokey, N. (1983)**. A comparison of tournaments and contracts. *JPE*, 91(3), 349–364 (common-shock cancellation).
- **Nalebuff, B. & Stiglitz, J. (1983)**. Prizes and incentives: towards a general theory of compensation and competition. *Bell JE*, 14(1), 21–43.
- **Chan, W. (1996)**. External recruitment versus internal promotion. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 14(4), 555–570 (sabotage).
- **Dye, R. (1984)**. The trouble with tournaments. *Economic Inquiry*, 22(1), 147–149 (sabotage).
- **Lazear, E. (1989)**. Pay equality and industrial politics. *JPE*, 97(3), 561–580 (sabotage/collusion).
- **Ehrenberg, R. & Bognanno, M. (1990)**. Do tournaments have incentive effects? *JPE*, 98(6), 1307–1324 (evidence).

nodes.title: A3. Fixed Wage + Efficiency Wage (Shapiro–Stiglitz 1984)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Keep $w_0 > w^{MC}$ (as in Weiss) **plus** monitoring probability $q$ + dismissal on detected shirking.

**Shapiro–Stiglitz no-shirking condition**:
$$w_0 - w^{MC} \;\geq\; \frac{c(e)\,(1-\delta)}{q\,\delta}$$

Wage premium must exceed effort cost adjusted by monitoring intensity. $e_i^{*} > 0$ induced by threat of losing the rent — not by output linkage.

---

**Signal**: none directly — pay is flat. Motivation from *threat of dismissal* under monitoring, plus wage above market-clearing so the job is worth keeping.

**Solves**
- Removes all output-based risk (F4).
- No metric to game → attacks multitasking (F2), Goodhart (F6).
- No incentive to hoard output → attacks cooperation collapse (F5).

**Breaks**
- Requires credible monitoring AND credible dismissal.
- Involuntary unemployment as equilibrium feature.
- No high-powered incentive → productivity ceiling.

**Use when**: output signals noisy or gameable; quality > quantity; firm has monitoring infrastructure.

---

### References

- **Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. (1984)**. Equilibrium unemployment as a worker discipline device. *AER*, 74(3), 433–444.
- **Yellen, J. (1984)**. Efficiency wage models of unemployment. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 74(2), 200–205 (survey).
- **Salop, S. (1979)**. A model of the natural rate of unemployment. *AER*, 69(1), 117–125 (turnover-cost variant).
- **Akerlof, G. (1982)**. Labor contracts as partial gift exchange. *QJE*, 97(4), 543–569.
- **Bulow, J. & Summers, L. (1986)**. A theory of dual labor markets. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 4(3), 376–414.
- **Krueger, A. & Summers, L. (1988)**. Efficiency wages and the inter-industry wage structure. *Econometrica*, 56(2), 259–293 (evidence).

nodes.title: A4. Team Pay / Profit Sharing (Kandel–Lazear 1992; Weitzman–Kruse 1990)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Add group-signal slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \beta_T \cdot s_{\text{team}}, \quad s_{\text{team}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \frac{\beta_T}{N}$$

Free-rider scales with $N$: individual reward on own effort $\propto 1/N$.

Kandel–Lazear (1992): peer pressure supplements the $1/N$ direct incentive for small $N$ — worker $i$ internalizes some cost of others' scrutiny.

---

**Signal**: group-level output — team quota, plant profits, firm profit.

**Solves**
- Rewards cooperation, mentoring, mutual help directly (F5).
- Aligns worker to firm value → attacks narrow-metric multitasking (F2).
- Peer pressure polices free-riders in small teams (Kandel–Lazear).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider problem grows with N — marginal reward on effort ≈ 1/N.
- Requires observability *between* peers so social pressure operates.
- Loads systematic risk (firm-wide shocks) onto workers — WORSENS F4.

**Use when**: small tight teams with strong cooperation externalities and mutual observability (surgical team, small startup).

---

### References

- **Kandel, E. & Lazear, E. (1992)**. Peer pressure and partnerships. *JPE*, 100(4), 801–817.
- **Weitzman, M. & Kruse, D. (1990)**. Profit sharing and productivity. In *Paying for Productivity*, Brookings.
- **Alchian, A. & Demsetz, H. (1972)**. Production, information costs, and economic organization. *AER*, 62(5), 777–795.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (free-rider theorem).
- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2013)**. Team incentives: evidence from a firm level experiment. *JEEA*, 11(5), 1079–1114.

nodes.title: A7. Subjective Evaluation + Bonus (MacLeod 2003; Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 1994)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Manager privately observes rating $m_i$ correlated with effort. Bonus $b(m_i)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + b(m_i)$$

Worker's effort FOC:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial b(m_i)}{\partial e_i}\right] = c'(e_i^{*})$$

Optimal $b^{*}$ (MacLeod 2003) balances effort inducement against **influence-activity** cost. Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit not to renege; reneging destroys the equilibrium.

---

**Signal**: manager's private assessment, converted to bonus/promotion.

**Solves**
- Manager can down-weight lucky outcomes and reward true effort → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Rewards multi-dim performance → attacks multitasking (F2).
- Preserves flexibility to reward cooperation, culture, mentoring (F5).
- No explicit threshold → no bunching (F6).

**Breaks**
- Influence activities (Milgrom 1988): workers persuade the manager instead of producing.
- Favoritism, discrimination, arbitrary variation.
- Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit to fair evaluation (MacLeod 2003).
- Legally hard to defend if evaluations diverge from measurables.

**Use when**: output is complex, multi-dimensional, hard to game via explicit metrics; long employment relationships with repeated interaction.

---

### References

- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240.
- **Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (1994)**. Subjective performance measures in optimal incentive contracts. *QJE*, 109(4), 1125–1156.
- **Milgrom, P. (1988)**. Employment contracts, influence activities, and efficient organization design. *JPE*, 96(1), 42–60.
- **Prendergast, C. & Topel, R. (1996)**. Favoritism in organizations. *JPE*, 104(5), 958–978.
- **Levin, J. (2003)**. Relational incentive contracts. *AER*, 93(3), 835–857.
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102.

nodes.title: A8. Ownership / Equity (Hansmann 1996; Kruse–Blasi 1997)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Add equity share $\phi \in (0,1)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \phi \cdot V, \qquad V = \sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \phi \cdot \frac{\partial V}{\partial e_i}$$

For workforce size $N$, effective incentive per worker on own task is $\phi/N$ — free-rider like team pay. But alignment with **long-run** firm value handles multi-dim + horizon simultaneously.

---

**Signal**: firm value — worker holds a residual claim (stock, options, partnership share, ESOP).

**Solves**
- Aligns effort with long-run firm value → solves multitasking (F2) and horizon jointly.
- Rewards firm-level cooperation and mentoring (F5).
- Long horizon smooths short-run bunching (F6).
- Prices cooperation externality → useful when Safelite condition #3 (individual production) fails (F7).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider grows with N (each worker owns ≈ 1/N).
- Loads undiversified risk onto workers (labor income + wealth co-move) — WORSENS F4.
- Governance costs — worker-owners may block value-creating layoffs.
- Requires liquidity / vesting to prevent early cash-out.

**Use when**: small firm, high-skill workers, long horizon, output primarily reflects team effort (early-stage startup, law/consulting partnership).

---

### References

- **Hansmann, H. (1996)**. *The Ownership of Enterprise*. Harvard University Press.
- **Kruse, D. & Blasi, J. (1997)**. Employee ownership, employee attitudes, and firm performance. In *The Human Resources Management Handbook*.
- **Jensen, M. & Meckling, W. (1976)**. Theory of the firm: managerial behavior, agency costs and ownership structure. *JFE*, 3(4), 305–360.
- **Blasi, J., Kruse, D. & Freeman, R. (2018)**. Broad-based employee stock ownership and profit sharing. *Journal of Participation and Employee Ownership*, 1(1), 38–60.
- **Oyer, P. (2004)**. Why do firms use incentives that have no incentive effects? *Journal of Finance*, 59(4), 1619–1650.

nodes.title: A9. Selection-Based Pay Structure (Lazear 1986, 2000)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

**No modification.** Selection IS the base mechanism — Weiss (1980) + PVR (2002) already sort $\theta$ via $w_0$ and $w(z)$.

A9's contribution: makes the sorting margin *explicit* in contract design. The CHOICE of $(w_0, \{\beta_j\})$ operates through sorting as much as through moral hazard.

Lazear (2000): about **half** of Safelite's 44% productivity gain came from sorting, not effort. Selection is the silent workhorse layered underneath every other alternative.

---

**Signal**: the *contract itself* acts as a filter — the pay structure attracts one type and repels another.

**Solves**
- You don't need to motivate ex-post; you need to attract the right type ex-ante.
- Lazear (2000): ~**half** of the Safelite 44% productivity gain was *sorting*, not effort.
- Reduces monitoring cost — the contract does the screening.
- Complementary to any base scheme; layers on top.

**Breaks**
- Requires labor-market heterogeneity and mobility.
- Sorting alone is often insufficient; usually combined with incentives.
- Can create adverse selection if the signal the contract offers is misread.

**Use when**: heterogeneous labor market, type unobservable directly, you want a self-enforcing filter. Note: this changes WHO applies, not what workers do once hired — so it doesn't fix any specific failure, it prevents them from arising.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (1986)**. Salaries and piece rates. *Journal of Business*, 59(3), 405–431.
- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (empirical decomposition: sorting vs incentive at Safelite).
- **Weiss, A. (1980)**. Job queues and layoffs in labor markets with flexible wages. *JPE*, 88(3), 526–538 (sorting via wage level).
- **Salop, S. & Salop, J. (1976)**. Self-selection and turnover in the labor market. *QJE*, 90(4), 619–627 (back-loaded pay as sorting).
- **Guasch, J. L. & Weiss, A. (1981)**. Self-selection in the labor market. *AER*, 71(3), 275–284.

nodes.title: F1. Imperfect Performance Measurement
nodes.content:
**Problem**

The signal we contract on is $s = g(\text{effort}) + \varepsilon$, not effort itself. Any noise $\varepsilon$ in the measurement gets transmitted into the worker's pay.

**Consequences**
- Risk-averse workers demand a wage premium for bearing noise → higher wage bill.
- Or firm dampens piece rate to reduce risk exposure → weaker incentive → less effort.
- Either way, first-best not achievable (Holmström–Milgrom 1987 optimal linear contract: risk vs incentive intensity tradeoff).

**Which alternatives address it**
- A2 Tournament (cancels common shock)
- A6 Career concerns (market averages many signals)
- A7 Subjective (manager corrects for luck)

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. (1979)**. Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10, 74–91.
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328.
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102.
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614.

nodes.title: F2. Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

If you reward one task among several, workers crowd out the un-rewarded tasks.

**Evidence**
- Asch (1990), Larkin (2014): piece rates on tasks A, B, C → worker picks only the mispriced (arbitrage) one.
- If firm tracks 3 tasks, worker finds the highest-marginal-return one and dumps the rest.

**Why**
Worker's cost of effort is convex; marginal reward differs across tasks. Optimal worker response is a corner solution unless firm equalizes marginal incentives across ALL relevant dimensions.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no metric to game)
- A4 Team pay (broader signal)
- A6 Career concerns (market prices overall ability)
- A7 Subjective (rewards all dimensions)
- A8 Ownership (aligned to firm value)

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, and job design. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52.
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614.
- **Asch, B. (1990)**. Do incentives matter? The case of Navy recruiters. *ILR Review*, 43(3), 89-S–106-S.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity in multi-task principal/agent relations. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.

nodes.title: F3. Ratchet Effect (Gibbons 1987)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Worker hides capacity — puts low effort in easy periods so the firm doesn't discover the task is easy and raise the quota next period. Roy (1952); Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005).

**Mechanism**
Worker's optimal effort today depends on how effort maps to *tomorrow's target*, not just today's pay. High output today → tighter quota tomorrow → dampen output.

**Classical fix (Holmström 1982; Shleifer 1985)**
Index quota to *peers*, not own history — own effort no longer feeds own standard. Yardstick competition. This is essentially A2 Tournament.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A2 Tournament (peer-indexed quotas)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon dilutes ratchet gain)
- A6 Career concerns (market has no reason to raise your standard)

---

### References

- **Gibbons, R. (1987)**. Piece-rate incentive schemes. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 5(4), 413–429.
- **Roy, D. (1952)**. Quota restriction and goldbricking in a machine shop. *American Journal of Sociology*, 57(5), 427–442.
- **Weitzman, M. (1980)**. The 'ratchet principle' and performance incentives. *Bell JE*, 11(1), 302–308 (Soviet planning context).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2007)**. Incentives for managers and inequality among workers: evidence from a firm-level experiment. *QJE*, 122(2), 729–773.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (yardstick / peer benchmark).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **Freixas, X., Guesnerie, R. & Tirole, J. (1985)**. Planning under incomplete information and the ratchet effect. *REStud*, 52(2), 173–191.

nodes.title: F4. Risk Transfer to Worker
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Pay = f(output). Output varies for reasons the worker cannot control: machine downtime, random customer arrivals, seasonal variation, task-difficulty heterogeneity.

**Consequence**
Risk-averse workers dislike income variance; they demand a risk premium. Firm pays MORE in expected wage bill for the same expected effort. The insurance-vs-incentive tradeoff (Holmström–Milgrom 1987) is the core of contract theory.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (removes ALL output risk)

**Which alternatives make it WORSE**
- A4 Team pay (loads systematic firm risk)
- A8 Ownership (undiversified: labor + wealth co-move)

---

### References

- **Ross, S. (1973)**. The economic theory of agency. *AER*, 63(2), 134–139.
- **Mirrlees, J. (1975/1999)**. The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. *REStud*, 66(1), 3–21.
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (risk-incentive tradeoff).
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102 (empirical test).
- **Ackerberg, D. & Botticini, M. (2002)**. Endogenous matching and the empirical determinants of contract form. *JPE*, 110(3), 564–591.

nodes.title: F5. Cooperation Collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003)
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
Garment plant switched from team pay to individual piece rates → total output FELL despite rising individual effort. Workers stopped teaching, helping, covering. Also Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer (2007) on physician groups.

**Mechanism**
Under piece rates, time spent helping a peer = zero personal reward + opportunity cost of your own output. Rational response: withdraw from cooperation. Knowledge transfer disappears.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (nothing to compete over)
- A4 Team pay (directly rewards cooperation)
- A7 Subjective (manager rewards mentoring)
- A8 Ownership (residual claim on joint output)

**Which alternatives make it WORSE**
- A2 Tournament (helping a peer is directly costly)

---

### References

- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity: garment plant evidence. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Encinosa, W., Gaynor, M. & Rebitzer, J. (2007)**. The sociology of groups and the economics of incentives. *JEBO*, 62(2), 187–214.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (peer effects).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2010)**. Social incentives in the workplace. *REStud*, 77(2), 417–458.
- **Freeman, R. & Medoff, J. (1984)**. *What Do Unions Do?* Basic Books (cooperation-through-voice).

nodes.title: F6. Goodhart / Bunching
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
- Oyer (1998): salespeople bunch deals before fiscal year-end.
- Larkin (2014): software sales *sandbag* large deals to avoid ratcheting next quarter.
- Camerer–Farber–Falk: taxi drivers, bike messengers stop at daily income target (backward-bending supply from loss aversion).

**Mechanism**
Any quota threshold creates a kink where marginal piece rate drops to zero (or turns negative via ratchet). Workers bunch AT the threshold — never above.

> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no threshold)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon smooths bunching)
- A6 Career concerns (continuous market pricing)
- A7 Subjective (no bright-line target)
- A8 Ownership (long-horizon claim)

---

### References

- **Goodhart, C. (1975)**. Problems of monetary management: the U.K. experience. Papers in Monetary Economics, Reserve Bank of Australia (origin of Goodhart's Law).
- **Oyer, P. (1998)**. Fiscal year ends and non-linear incentive contracts. *QJE*, 113(1), 149–185.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Camerer, C., Babcock, L., Loewenstein, G. & Thaler, R. (1997)**. Labor supply of New York City cab drivers: one day at a time. *QJE*, 112(2), 407–441.
- **Farber, H. (2015)**. Why you can't find a taxi in the rain and other labor supply lessons from cab drivers. *QJE*, 130(4), 1975–2026.
- **Chevalier, J. & Ellison, G. (1997)**. Risk taking by mutual funds as a response to incentives. *JPE*, 105(6), 1167–1200 (kink-driven behavior).

nodes.title: F7. Safelite Preconditions (when piece rate works)
nodes.content:
**Three conditions that made Safelite work**

1. **Output perfectly measurable**: install-a-windshield-or-not; discrete, countable, homogeneous.
2. **Quality standard clear**: any leak/failure → worker returns to fix, unpaid, on own time. Solves the quality-quantity multitasking problem via ex-post penalty.
3. **Production individual**: no cooperation externalities to destroy. One worker, one car, one windshield.

**Implication for Quindi.AI**: violates #3 (cooperation matters) and possibly #1 (multi-dim AI-assisted output). Price cooperation, don't rely on a single scalar throughput.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study — the original documentation of the preconditions).
- **Paarsch, H. & Shearer, B. (1999)**. The response of worker effort to piece rates: evidence from the British Columbia tree-planting industry. *JHR*, 34(4), 643–667 (another individual, measurable, quality-easy-to-monitor setting).
- **Shearer, B. (2004)**. Piece rates, fixed wages and incentives: evidence from a field experiment. *REStud*, 71(2), 513–534.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (breakdown when preconditions fail).

nodes.title: ★ ABM Theory — Core
nodes.content:
# ABM Theory — Core

## Why ABM?

Analytical incentive models (HM 1987 etc.) buy tractability with assumptions that fail for Quindi:

| Analytical assumption | Reality at Quindi |
|---|---|
| Representative agent | **Heterogeneous** workers: ability, risk aversion, peer network, reciprocity |
| Common knowledge, rationality | **Bounded rationality**; workers use heuristics |
| No interaction / mean-field | **Peer effects, cooperation, sabotage** matter |
| Equilibrium closed-form | **Out-of-equilibrium** transitions (rollouts, contract switches) |
| Same $\beta$ for all agents | We can see how **heterogeneous agents** react to incentives |
| Task assignment fixed / exogenous | Firm **reorganises tasks** in response to worker fit — Quindi's lever 1 |

**ABM (Agent-Based Model)** relaxes each: simulate a population of heterogeneous agents whose behavior is specified by rules, let interactions unfold, and observe emergent outcomes.

## What we simulate — Quindi's two levers

Quindi delivers two independent treatments:

1. **Reorganisation** — firm reassigns workers to best-fit tasks, holding contract fixed.
2. **Incentives** — firm switches contract from $A_0$ (flat wage) to $A_j$, holding task assignment fixed.

Each is a switchable channel. The ABM lets us toggle them independently and observe per-worker productivity, cooperation, wage bill, and — crucially — the **bias of the naive causal estimator** for each channel.

---

## What ABM adds over analytical PA

- **Heterogeneity**: workers differ in $(\varepsilon_i, \rho_i, k_i, \phi_i, \delta_i)$.
- **Rules over optima**: agents follow behavioral rules; effort $e_i$ is the equilibrium of those rules given the contract.
- **Interactions**: peer effects, help/sabotage, network diffusion.
- **Emergence**: aggregate output, wage dispersion, cooperation clusters emerge; they are not assumed.
- **Out-of-equilibrium**: treatment (AI rollout) and contract switches can be studied without new equilibrium assumptions.
- **Empirical calibration**: rules calibrated to observed micro-data (BBR 2005; Mas–Moretti 2009).

---

## Design taxonomy — how ABM agents decide

Agents' decisions can be modelled in five styles, in increasing sophistication:

| Approach | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed heuristics** | Static formula (e.g., markup pricing) | Dawid EURACE; Boudreau 2010 |
| **Discrete choice** | Random-utility logit / probit | Neugart 2008; Martin–Neugart 2009 |
| **Adaptive rules** | Rule updates parameters from experience | Richiardi 2006 |
| **Reinforcement learning** | Q-learning / softmax update | Gemkow–Neugart 2011 |
| **Optimising** | Solve Bellman (rare in ABM) | Standard DSGE-adjacent |

Quindi ABM uses a mix: **adaptive rules** for effort; **discrete choice** for menu decisions (help whom, accept promotion); **RL** for slow-feedback decisions (cooperation investment).

---

## Behavioral mechanisms — why agents under-produce

Ten literature-backed mechanisms; agents' equilibrium effort is the joint response to all:

1. **Shirking under flat wage** — Shapiro–Stiglitz 1984 → $e^* = 0$.
2. **Free-riding in teams** — Alchian–Demsetz 1972; Kandel–Lazear 1992 → $\partial w/\partial e = \beta_T/n$.
3. **Multitasking arbitrage** — HM 1991 → $e_j = 0$ if $\beta_j = 0$.
4. **Ratchet hiding** — Gibbons 1987 → under-produce to hide capacity.
5. **Tournament sabotage** — Chan 1996; Lazear 1989 → $\sigma_{ij}^* > 0$.
6. **Loss-averse Goodhart bunching** — Kahneman–Tversky 1979; Camerer et al. 1997.
7. **Reciprocity / gift exchange** — Akerlof 1982; Fehr–Falk 2002 → $e = e^{\text{base}} + \phi(w - \bar w)$.
8. **Peer conformity** — BBR 2005/2010; Mas–Moretti 2009.
9. **Career-concern signalling** — Holmström 1982; Gibbons–Murphy 1992.
10. **Cooperation externality** — Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003 → $a_{ij}^* = 0$ under piece rate.

Each is a switchable module in the simulation.

---

## Simulation architecture — 2×2 counterfactual

Four cells per seed, one per combination of the two levers:

| Cell | Reorg | Incentive | Assignment | Contract | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B** (0,0) | Off | Off | $\mu_0$ | $A_0$ | $e = 0$ |
| **R** (1,0) | **On** | Off | $\mu^*$ | $A_0$ | $e = 0$ |
| **I** (0,1) | Off | **On** | $\mu_0$ | $A_j$ | $e = e^*$ |
| **F** (1,1) | **On** | **On** | $\mu^*$ | $A_j$ | $e = e^*$ |

Same population, same shocks, same seed across cells (common random numbers).

### Causal estimands

$$\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} = Y_R - Y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{incent}} = Y_I - Y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{total}} = Y_F - Y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{interaction}} = \hat\tau_{\text{total}} - \hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} - \hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$$

Structural truths (set inside the sim) let us compute **bias per estimand per contract**.

### Time step (one period)

1. Firm assigns tasks via $\mu$ (chosen by cell).
2. Contract announces state (rank, targets, monitoring).
3. Workers choose $(e_i, a_{ij}, \sigma_{ij})$ as best response given behavioural rules.
4. Signals realise; team + firm output computed.
5. Wages paid; workers update beliefs and reference points.

### Robustness sweeps

Grid over $(\rho, n, \text{network topology}, k, \sigma^2, \text{task portfolio structure}, \pi)$. Identify parameter regions where each estimand is trusted.

---

## Tech stack

**Python 3.11 + Mesa 2.x**. Alternatives: Julia + Agents.jl (speed), NetLogo (prototyping), ML3 (formal DSL — see paper snippet).

Repo: `agents.py`, `contracts.py`, `network.py`, `model.py`, `simulate.py`, `measure.py`, `analysis.ipynb`, `config.yaml`.

Scale target: $N = 10{,}000$, $T = 500$, 20 contracts, 100 seeds → feasible overnight on one machine.

---

## Prior-work gap

No published paper implements **all A1–A9 as swappable modules in one ABM with per-contract ATE identification analysis**. Closest neighbours: Axtell 2001 (firm emergence); EURACE (many contracts, no ATE); Squazzoni 2014 (cooperation, no identification). Building this for Quindi is a genuine contribution.

---

## Literature map — one paper snippet per node

Follow arrows from this core to individual paper snippets:

| Snippet | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **P·Bergmann 1974** | Original micro-simulation of the macroeconomy |
| **P·Axtell 2001** | Firm emergence + free-riding (closest ancestor) |
| **P·EURACE (Dawid et al. 2008–12)** | Full macro ABM with mgmt-science rules |
| **P·K+S (Dosi–Fagiolo–Roventini 2010)** | Keynes + Schumpeter macro ABM |
| **P·CATS (Delli Gatti et al. 2011)** | Bottom-up macroeconomics ABM |
| **P·Fagiolo–Dosi–Gabriele 2004** | Evolutionary labor-market ABM |
| **P·Neugart 2008** | Discrete-choice job search / policy |
| **P·Martin–Neugart 2009** | Discrete-choice wage-setting |
| **P·Richiardi 2006** | Adaptive-rule job search |
| **P·Gemkow–Neugart 2011** | RL for network investment |
| **P·Boudreau 2010** | Rank-imitation human-capital rule |
| **P·ML3 (Reinhardt et al. 2022)** | Formal DSL for linked-lives ABM |
| **P·Rivkin–Siggelkow 2003** | 3-tier org ABM (workers × middle × top) |
| **P·Levinthal 1997** | NK-landscape organisational adaptation |
| **P·Neugart–Richiardi 2018** | Handbook survey — design patterns |

---

## Bottom line

- ABM relaxes the 3 crippling assumptions of analytical PA (representative agent, common knowledge, no interaction).
- Agents follow behavioural rules (fixed / discrete choice / adaptive / RL / optimising).
- Ten literature-backed mechanisms explain under-production; each is switchable.
- Contract A0–A9 is a plug-in module; per-contract ATE bias is the key output.
- Genuine research contribution: no published paper combines all these elements.

Founding **micro-simulation of the whole macroeconomy** with agent-level firms, workers, banks, government.

Each period: firms plan → hire → produce → price → pay taxes → invest → finance; workers earn → consume → save; banks + monetary authority intermediate. All flows tracked explicitly.

**Ref.** Axtell, R. (2001). Effort dynamics in economic organizations. *SFI Working Paper 99-11-076*; later in various venues.

## Contribution
ABM where **firms emerge endogenously** from workers' effort/free-riding choices.

## Idea
Agents voluntarily form firms. Each agent chooses effort trading own income vs shirking. Firms grow if effort high enough; collapse otherwise.

## Result
Reproduces empirical firm-size distribution (Zipf's law) endogenously. Explains firm dynamics through effort–free-rider tension.

nodes.title: P·Neugart (2008) — Discrete Choice
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Neugart, M. (2008). Labor market policy evaluation with ACE. *Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization*, 67(2), 418–430.

---

# Neugart (2008) — Discrete-Choice Agent-Based Labor Market

**ACE** = Agent-based Computational Economics. Neugart shows that thousands of individual **discrete-choice** decisions, calibrated to real micro-data, can substitute for representative-agent optimisation in labor-market policy analysis.

## Why discrete choice in ABM?

Between the two extremes of (a) full dynamic optimisation (intractable at scale) and (b) fixed heuristics (arbitrary), discrete choice sits comfortably in the middle:

- Agents face a **finite menu** of alternatives $\{1, 2, \ldots, J\}$.
- Each has a utility $U_{ij} = V_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}$, where $V_{ij}$ is the systematic part (function of observables) and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is idiosyncratic noise.
- Under EV1 (Gumbel) noise, the choice probability is the **multinomial logit** (McFadden 1974):
$$P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(V_{ij})}{\sum_{k=1}^{J} \exp(V_{ik})}$$

The agent doesn't solve a Bellman equation — she flips a probabilistic coin whose weights encode her preferences.

## What Neugart 2008 does

**Setup**: a labor market populated by heterogeneous workers (age, skill, tenure, unemployment history) and firms (productivity, size). Search frictions à la Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides but implemented at the individual level.

**Every decision is a discrete choice**:
- Worker: accept a job offer? enroll in training? change occupation?
- Firm: post vacancy? hire this applicant? offer training subsidy?

Each choice's systematic utility $V_{ij}$ depends on the state of the individual (wage offer vs reservation wage, tenure, past experience) and current policy parameters (subsidy level, unemployment insurance replacement rate).

## Empirical calibration

The critical step: **coefficients on $V_{ij}$ are estimated from real German micro-data** (SOEP, LFS, IAB). Every logit coefficient corresponds to a parameter with an economic meaning that can be pinned down from observed choices.

This gives the ABM two properties that Bellman-based models lack:

1. **Empirical anchor**: the aggregate behavior is disciplined by observation, not just theory.
2. **Behavioural realism**: agents make mistakes with probabilities matching real workers' inconsistencies.

## What the simulation produces

Thousands of individual logit draws, aggregated:

- Time-series of unemployment rate, vacancy rate, wages.
- Response to policy shocks (raise training subsidy → observe transition dynamics).
- Distributional consequences (who benefits from a policy? who loses?).

Because the coefficients are calibrated, the aggregate response can be validated against observed policy effects from natural experiments.

## Why it matters — three points

1. **Bridge between econometrics and ABM.** Discrete-choice models are the workhorse of empirical labor economics; Neugart shows they slot cleanly into an ABM without loss of interpretability.
2. **Policy evaluation without representative agent.** You can compare policy $A$ vs policy $B$ under **realistic heterogeneity** — no assumption of a single agent representing all workers.
3. **Computational scalability.** A logit choice is $O(J)$ per agent per period. Millions of agents × decades of periods is feasible.

## Limitations

- **Fixed rule**: coefficients don't update as agents learn. This is a Lucas-critique concern for large policy shifts.
- **Menu specification**: the analyst must enumerate alternatives; agents can't discover new options.
- **Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives (IIA)**: standard logit has restrictive substitution patterns; nested logit or mixed logit relax this.

## Where it sits in the ABM design space

```
Fixed heuristics ── Discrete choice ── RL / adaptive ── Optimising
    (Dawid)         (Neugart 2008;      (Richiardi;     (Standard DSGE)
    (Boudreau)      Martin–Neugart)     Gemkow–Neugart)
```

Discrete choice trades some flexibility (rules don't learn) for **empirical discipline** (coefficients from data). It's the natural entry point for anyone doing serious labor-market ABM work.

## Relevance for the Quindi ABM

Directly applicable to **menu decisions** in Quindi's simulation:

- Worker: accept the AI treatment (if voluntary) — logit.
- Worker: which peer to help — logit over $\mathcal{N}_i$.
- Worker: which task to pull from queue — logit over tasks.
- Worker: accept promotion to L1 — logit.
- Manager: which applicant to promote — logit over candidates.

Coefficients can be calibrated from Quindi's own operational data (past acceptance decisions, past promotion outcomes). This is the empirical-anchor route to keep the ABM disciplined.

## Bottom line

Neugart 2008 is the **canonical example of a discrete-choice ABM in labor economics**. It shows that empirically-calibrated logit rules can substitute for full optimisation, are computationally cheap, and deliver policy-relevant simulations. For any ABM decision that can be framed as "choose one of $J$ alternatives", this is the right template.

→ Anchor: **ABM Theory Core**

**Ref.** Richiardi, M. (2006). Toward a non-equilibrium unemployment theory. *Computational Economics*, 27(1), 135–160.

Workers decide whether to search this period. Instead of solving a Bellman equation (McCall model), they use a rule that updates from past experience (temporal-difference learning).

**Reinforcement learning** applied to network investment.

nodes.title: P·ML3 (Reinhardt–Warnke–Uhrmacher 2022)
nodes.content:
**Ref.** Reinhardt, O., Warnke, T. & Uhrmacher, A. M. (2022). A formal foundation for the modeling language ML3. *ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation (TOMACS)*, 32(1), Article 6.

---

# ML3 — Modeling Language for Linked Lives

**ML3** is a domain-specific formal modeling language developed at the **University of Rostock** (Reinhardt, Warnke, Uhrmacher) for building agent-based demographic simulations — particularly ones where people's life events (birth, marriage, migration, retirement, death) are *linked* to those of others through networks.

## What "linked lives" means

The core insight — borrowed from life-course sociology (Elder, Bengtson) — is that individual demographic trajectories are **not independent**:

- my migration decision depends on whether my spouse migrated,
- my job depends on my parents' education,
- my death rate depends on my caregiver's presence.

Traditional micro-simulation models treated agents independently. **ML3 makes those *connections* first-class.**

## Three design decisions that make ML3 distinctive

### 1. Discrete events in continuous time

Not the discrete-time step model of NetLogo / Mesa ("every day, workers decide…"). Instead, agents undergo events at **real-valued time points** drawn from probability distributions.

Example: "birth of first child happens at age $t \sim \text{Weibull}(\alpha, \beta)$ given fertility". This matches demography naturally — you don't want children born only at integer ages.

### 2. Age-specific AND deterministic events

Some events fire at a **fixed age**: retirement at 65, mandatory schooling entry at 6, election eligibility at 18. These are **deterministic**, not stochastic.

Standard **Continuous-Time Markov Chains** (CTMCs) can't express this — CTMCs assume all transitions are exponentially distributed (memoryless). ML3 handles both: stochastic events *and* deterministic scheduled events.

The correct mathematical framework isn't a CTMC — it's a **Generalized Semi-Markov Process (GSMP)**, which the paper formally maps ML3 models to.

### 3. Agents connected via network edges

Every ML3 agent has references to other agents (spouses, parents, children, neighbors, employers). Events on one agent can trigger events on connected agents.

Example: *if a person's spouse dies, adjust the person's residence transition rate*.

## What ML3 is NOT (comparison)

| Framework | Time | Events | Structure | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NetLogo / Mesa** | Discrete steps | Simple | Grid or network | Prototyping, teaching |
| **CTMC-based (e.g., PRISM)** | Continuous | Memoryless (exp) | Flat | Verifiable stochastic systems |
| **DEVS** | Continuous | Discrete | **Hierarchical** | Engineering, aerospace |
| **ML3** | Continuous | Stochastic **+ deterministic + age-specific** | Flat network | **Demography, life-course** |
| **Agents.jl (Julia)** | Discrete or continuous | Custom | Flat or network | Performance-critical ABM |

The two design frontiers ML3 addresses:
- **DEVS is *too hierarchical*** for demography (people aren't inside a "family module" inside a "neighborhood module"; they're just linked).
- **CTMCs can't handle *deterministic timing*** like retirement age.

## What ML3 gives you concretely

Each agent has:
- **Attributes** (age, sex, employment, income, …)
- **Links** to other agents ("spouse", "employer", …)
- **Rules** of the form:

```
rule: person p, age a ~ Weibull(k, λ) →
   marry(p, findPartnerFromNetwork(p));
   attribute p.status := "married"
```

The scheduler resolves the **earliest event** across all agents in continuous time (à la Gillespie / discrete-event simulation), fires it, updates state, recomputes next-event times.

## Why the formal semantics matters (this paper's contribution)

Before this 2022 paper, ML3 was described **informally** — meaning by examples and reference implementation only. That's a serious problem for scientific ABMs:

- **Reproducibility**: another researcher can't check if their re-implementation is semantically equivalent.
- **Verification**: you can't prove properties of the model.
- **Composition**: you can't safely combine sub-models.

The 2022 paper gives ML3 a rigorous **mathematical semantics** (mapping to GSMPs), so any implementation can be checked against the spec. **This is the standard demography ABMs previously lacked.**

## Where ML3 sits in the ABM landscape

```
General-purpose         Domain-specific
     ▲                        ▲
     │                        │
Mesa, NetLogo             ML3 (demography)
Agents.jl                 EURACE (macro)
DEVS                      
     │                        │
     ▼                        ▼
   Flexible                Specialized,
   but generic             but sharper
```

## Relevance for the Quindi ABM

ML3 is a plausible choice **if**:
- Career events (promotion, resignation, hire, fire) happen in **continuous time** and shouldn't be forced to integer weeks.
- Some events are **age-linked** (retirement, seniority-based pay under A5 deferred compensation).
- Agents are connected via **stable networks** (worker-to-L1 manager, L1-to-top) that shape outcomes.

If those apply, ML3 gives you a mathematically clean foundation. If you're okay with discrete time steps and simpler formal foundations, **Mesa** (Python) or **Agents.jl** (Julia) are more practical.

**For research-grade demography-style rigor: ML3.**

## Bottom line

The paper's contribution isn't a new modelling paradigm — it's providing a **rigorous, verifiable specification** for a corner of ABM (continuous-time, deterministic + age-specific events, network-linked agents) that other ABM frameworks handle awkwardly.

→ Anchor: **ABM Theory Core**

nodes.title: ★ Causal Identification — Empirical
nodes.content:
# Causal Identification with Empirical Data

Quindi has two levers. Post-rollout at a client, we observe joint outcomes and need to attribute them cleanly.

## The core problem

If Quindi turns on BOTH levers at once, the naïve difference-in-means $\bar y_{Q=1} - \bar y_{Q=0}$ blends:

1. **Incentive effect** (same worker on same task, more effort).
2. **Reorganisation effect** (better task assignment).
3. **Selection** (high-skill teams adopt Quindi first).
4. **Contract-induced gaming** (F2, F3, F5, F6).

Disentangling requires a **research design**.

---

## Strategy 1 — 2×2 factorial RCT (best)

Randomise two treatments independently across client teams:

| Arm | Reorganisation | Incentive contract |
|---|---|---|
| **B** (0, 0) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **R** (1, 0) | **Quindi reorganises** to $\mu^*$ | Flat wage $A_0$ |
| **I** (0, 1) | Old assignment $\mu_0$ | **Quindi contract $A_j$** |
| **F** (1, 1) | **Quindi reorganises** + **Quindi contract** | |

Estimation (identification is clean by random assignment):

$$\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} = \bar y_R - \bar y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{incent}} = \bar y_I - \bar y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{total}} = \bar y_F - \bar y_B$$
$$\hat\tau_{\text{interaction}} = \hat\tau_{\text{total}} - \hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} - \hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$$

**Sell to clients as three separate mini-products**: reorg-only, incentive-only, full-stack. Each arm is a legitimate offering.

---

## Strategy 2 — Staged rollout (near-best)

If 2×2 is politically hard, run in phases:

- **Phase 1** (months 1–3): random $A_j$ treatment, **assignment frozen** at $\mu_0$ → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.
- **Phase 2** (months 4–6): allow Quindi to reorganise → clean $\hat\tau_{\text{total}}$, then $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}} = \hat\tau_{\text{total}} - \hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$.

**Assumption**: incentive effect stable across phases.

---

## Strategy 3 — Within-worker-within-task fixed effects (observational)

Panel data with workers doing multiple tasks over time; some clients adopt one Quindi module before the other (staggered adoption):

$$y_{ikt} \;=\; \alpha_i + \gamma_k + \delta_t + \tau_{\text{incent}} \cdot Q^{\text{incent}}_{it} + \tau_{\text{reorg}} \cdot Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it} + \varepsilon_{ikt}$$

where $y_{ikt}$ is output of worker $i$ on task $k$ at time $t$; $Q^{\text{incent}}_{it}$, $Q^{\text{reorg}}_{it}$ are module-adoption indicators.

- $\tau_{\text{incent}}$ identified from same $(i, k)$ pre vs post contract switch.
- $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ identified from worker crossing tasks under stable contract.

**Assumptions**: task-switching orthogonal to shock $\varepsilon$ given FEs; parallel trends; no learning-by-doing bias.

---

## Strategy 4 — Structural production function (robustness)

Fit $y_i = f(\varepsilon_i, \tau_{\mu(i)}, Q_i, e_i; \theta)$; identify $\theta$ from moments; simulate counterfactuals with $\mu$ frozen. Roy-model / assignment-model tradition (Sattinger 1993; Heckman–Honoré 1990; Costinot–Vogel 2010).

Use only as **cross-check** on Strategies 1–3.

---

## Threats to identification (common to all strategies)

1. **Learning-by-doing**: workers improve regardless of Quindi. Control with tenure + pre-trends.
2. **Peer spillovers**: untreated workers observe treated peers. Cluster by team; use saturation design.
3. **Compliance**: managers deviate from randomised protocol. Report ITT + LATE (IV with assignment as instrument).
4. **Task-mix drift**: incoming workload composition shifts. Match on task composition.
5. **Selection into task-switching**: managers move stars first. Fixed effects only fix time-invariant selection.

---

## Recommendation for Quindi (paper 1 → paper 2)

- **Paper 1 (Incentive lever)**: run **Phase 1 of Strategy 2** — randomise $A_j$ across teams; freeze task assignment. Publish $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$ under each $A_j$.
- **Paper 2 (Reorganisation lever)**: run **Phase 2** — allow Quindi reorganisation on the treated arm. Publish $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ + interaction.

Strategy 3 (FE) as a robustness check on both. Strategy 4 for structural counterfactuals.

---

### References

- **Angrist & Pischke (2009, 2015)** — *Mostly Harmless Econometrics* / *Mastering Metrics*. Standard reference on RCT + FE + IV.
- **Duflo, Glennerster & Kremer (2007)** — *Using randomization in development economics research*. RCT design.
- **Bertrand, Duflo & Mullainathan (2004, QJE)** — clustered inference in DiD.
- **Card & Krueger (1994, AER)** — natural-experiment identification.
- **Sattinger (1993, JEL)** — assignment models (foundation for the reorg-lever structural check).
- **Heckman & Honoré (1990, Econometrica)** — Roy model identification.
- **Costinot & Vogel (2010, JPE)** — assignment and trade with heterogeneous workers.
- **Chetty, Friedman & Rockoff (2014, AER)** — teacher value-added under fixed pay.

→ Anchor: **ABM Theory Core** (for the causal-ABM version of these strategies).

nodes.title: ★ Causal Identification — ABM
nodes.content:
# Causal Identification in the ABM

In simulation, every empirical identification strategy reduces to a **config-file switch**. This snippet mirrors the Empirical snippet, one strategy at a time, and shows what the ABM adds that empirical work cannot: **direct validation against the known structural truth**.

---

## Strategy 1 in ABM — 2×2 factorial

```python
for seed in seeds:
    population = draw_workers(seed)     # same across cells
    shocks     = draw_shocks(seed, T)   # same across cells

    for cell in [(0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1)]:
        reorg_on, incent_on = cell

        mu       = firm.optimise_assignment(pop) if reorg_on  else mu_0
        contract = A_j                          if incent_on else A_0

        y = simulate(pop, shocks, mu, contract, seed)
        log(seed, cell, y)

# Estimation
tau_reorg  = mean(y | cell=(1,0)) - mean(y | cell=(0,0))
tau_incent = mean(y | cell=(0,1)) - mean(y | cell=(0,0))
tau_total  = mean(y | cell=(1,1)) - mean(y | cell=(0,0))
```

**Cost**: 4× simulation runs per seed. Trivial.

---

## Strategy 2 in ABM — staged rollout

Run phases sequentially with the same seed:

```python
phase1 = simulate(reorg=False, incent=True,  A_j, seed)  # → tau_incent
phase2 = simulate(reorg=True,  incent=True,  A_j, seed)  # → tau_total
tau_reorg = phase2 - phase1
```

Cross-check: does this recover the same $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ as the 2×2? If yes → Strategy 2 is valid in the empirical rollout. If not → the 'incentive effect stable across phases' assumption is broken.

---

## Strategy 3 in ABM — within-worker-within-task FE

Generate a panel with staggered adoption; run the FE regression on the simulated log:

```python
for seed in seeds:
    population = draw_workers(seed)
    # Staggered rollout: some workers get incentive at t=5, reorg at t=10; some vice versa; some never
    adoption = draw_staggered_adoption(pop, seed)

    for t in range(T):
        for i in workers:
            k = mu_panel[i, t]
            Q_incent = adoption[i, 'incent'] <= t
            Q_reorg  = adoption[i, 'reorg']  <= t
            y = produce(i, k, Q_incent, Q_reorg, effort=e[i,t])
            log(seed, i, k, t, y, Q_incent, Q_reorg)

# Estimation via linearmodels
fe = PanelOLS.from_formula(
    'y ~ Q_incent + Q_reorg + EntityEffects + TimeEffects',
    data=df.set_index(['worker_task', 't'])
).fit()

tau_incent_hat = fe.params['Q_incent']
tau_reorg_hat  = fe.params['Q_reorg']
```

---

## The killer feature — bias against known truth

The ABM sets $\tau_{\text{incent}}^{\text{structural}}$ and $\tau_{\text{reorg}}^{\text{structural}}$ inside the simulation. After each strategy, compute:

$$\text{bias}_{s} \;=\; \hat\tau_{s} - \tau^{\text{structural}}$$

Typical output:

| Strategy | Assumption tested | $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$ | truth | bias | $\hat\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ | truth | bias |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. 2×2** | Random assignment | 20.1% | 20% | +0.1% ✅ | 8.2% | 8% | +0.2% ✅ |
| **2. Staged** | Stable incentive across phases | 20.0% | 20% | 0% ✅ | 7.5% | 8% | −0.5% ✅ |
| **3. FE** | Task-switch exogenous \| FE | 22.3% | 20% | +2.3% ⚠️ | 9.6% | 8% | +1.6% ⚠️ |
| **Naive DiD** | none | 33% | 20% | +13% ❌ | — | — | — |

---

## Stress-test the strategies inside the ABM

Because you control the DGP, break assumptions and re-run:

```python
scenarios = [
    'baseline',
    'endogenous_task_switching',   # managers move stars first
    'learning_by_doing',           # workers improve with tenure
    'peer_spillovers',             # SUTVA violated
    'compliance_15pct',            # 15% of teams deviate from RCT protocol
]

for scenario in scenarios:
    for strategy in [S1, S2, S3]:
        biases[scenario, strategy] = run_and_estimate(scenario, strategy)
```

Produces a **bias grid**: which strategy survives which threat.

| Scenario | Strategy 1 bias | Strategy 2 bias | Strategy 3 bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | ~0% | ~0% | ~2% |
| + endogenous switching | ~0% | ~0% | **+8%** ⚠️ |
| + learning by doing | ~0% | +2% (contamination) | +5% |
| + peer spillovers | +3% (SUTVA) | +3% | +4% |
| + 15% non-compliance | ~0% (ITT) | +5% | +6% |

**Report to Quindi**: "In your typical client environment, use Strategy 1 if possible (biases < 3% under all threats). If Strategy 3 is your only option, expect +5–8% upward bias on $\hat\tau_{\text{incent}}$; report confidence intervals accordingly."

---

## What the ABM gives you that empirical work cannot

| Quantity | Empirical | ABM |
|---|---|---|
| True $\tau_{\text{incent}}$, $\tau_{\text{reorg}}$ | **Unknown** | **Known (set in config)** |
| Bias of estimator | **Unknown** (no ground truth) | **Directly measurable** |
| Sensitivity to confounders | Requires natural experiment | Set them on/off in config |
| Power calculations | Simulate under assumed effect | Simulate under known effect |
| Interaction effects | Requires 2×2 in real world | Trivial: cell (1,1) − others |

The ABM's *identification purpose* is to tell Quindi **which empirical strategy to invest in for each client**, and by how much each strategy would lie in that client's specific environment.

---

### References

- **Neugart & Richiardi (2018)** — ABM validation patterns.
- **Manski (2003, 2007)** — partial identification bounds (useful when strategies give conflicting estimates).
- **Chesher (2010)** — instrumental identification in structural models.
- **Athey & Imbens (2017, JEP)** — the state of applied econometrics — ML meets causal inference.
- **Bertrand, Duflo, Mullainathan (2004)** — clustered SE for panel DiD.

→ Anchor: **ABM Theory Core**

nodes.title: ★ Optimal Quindi Reward Formula
nodes.content:
# Optimal Quindi Reward Formula

## Umbrella frame (Holmström–Milgrom 1987)

> Under CARA + Gaussian noise, the optimal linear contract is $w = \alpha + \beta \cdot s$, where $s$ is a **signal vector**. Piece rates = a specific $(\beta, s)$; tournaments = ranking-based $s$; profit share = team $s$. The design choice is **what signal $s$** you contract on and **whose $s$** (self, peer, team, firm).

## Signal vector for Quindi

Four signals, each targeting a distinct failure family:

| # | Signal | Definition | Whose | Fixes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $s_3$ | Peer-relative combined index (quantity + quality) | $[q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}] + \lambda [Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}}]$ | Self vs peers | **F1**, **F2**, **F3** |
| $s_4$ | Cooperation signal | mentoring hits, help-given, knowledge-share flags | Self + peer-reported | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_5$ | Team output | small-team KPI ($N \approx 5$) | Team | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_6$ | Subjective manager rating | manager's assessment | Manager | **F1**, **F2**, **F6** |

Definitions:
- $q_i$ = individual throughput (calls closed, tickets resolved),
- $Q_i$ = individual quality (CSAT, error rate, rework),
- $\bar q_{\text{peers}}, \bar Q_{\text{peers}}$ = peer-group means,
- $\lambda > 0$ = relative price of quality vs quantity.

## Contract

$$\boxed{\; w_i \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \beta_3\, s_{3}(i) \;+\; \beta_4\, s_{4}(i) \;+\; \beta_5\, s_{5} \;+\; \beta_6\, s_{6}(i) \;}$$

Unpacked:

$$
w_i \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{floor (F4)}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 \big[(q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}) + \lambda (Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}})\big]}_{\text{peer-relative Q+Q, F1/F2/F3}} + \underbrace{\beta_4\, s_{4}(i)}_{\text{cooperation, F5}} + \underbrace{\beta_5\, s_{5}}_{\text{team share, F5/F7}} + \underbrace{\beta_6\, s_{6}(i)}_{\text{subjective, F1/F2/F6}}
$$

## Optimal weight vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$

From Holmström–Milgrom (1991) multitasking:

$$\boxed{\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*} \;=\; \big(I + \rho\, C\, \Sigma\big)^{-1}\, \mathbf{g}' \;}$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)^\top$ and
- $\mathbf{g}' = (\partial V / \partial e_j)_{j\in\{3,4,5,6\}}$ — marginal firm value of effort on each dim,
- $C$ — effort-cost Hessian ($4 \times 4$),
- $\Sigma$ — noise covariance of $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$,
- $\rho$ — CARA risk aversion of workforce.

**Reading it**:
- $\Sigma_{jj} \uparrow$ (noisier signal) $\Rightarrow \beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: don't pay heavily on noisy signals.
- Off-diagonal $\Sigma_{jk} > 0$ (correlated) $\Rightarrow$ down-weight the noisier of the pair.
- $\rho \uparrow$ (risk-averse) $\Rightarrow$ all $\beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: shift toward fixed pay $\alpha$.

**Balance condition** (no dimension arbitrable):

$$\frac{\beta_j^{*}}{\beta_k^{*}} \;=\; \frac{g_j' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_j^2\, k_j / g_j'^{\,2})}{g_k' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_k^2\, k_k / g_k'^{\,2})}$$

## Optimal $\lambda^{*}$

Set $\lambda$ so quantity and quality generate equal marginal firm value:

$$\lambda^{*} \;=\; \frac{\partial V / \partial Q}{\partial V / \partial q}$$

## Estimating parameters from Quindi data

- **$\sigma_j^2$** — residual variance of $s_j$ after netting worker fixed effects.
- **$\rho$** — risk-preference survey OR back out via WTA in current pay.
- **$k_j = c_{jj}''$** — labor-supply elasticity: within-worker effort response to bonus variation.
- **$g_j'$** — firm-level regression $V = \sum_j g_j'\, s_j + \varepsilon$.

With $(\rho, \Sigma, C, \mathbf{g}', \lambda)$ estimated, $\boldsymbol\beta^{*}$ is a closed-form matrix computation.

## What this contract accomplishes

| Failure | Fixed via |
|---|---|
| **F1** measurement | $s_3$ peer-relative (common shock cancelled) + $s_6$ subjective correction |
| **F2** multitasking | Balanced $\boldsymbol\beta$ across all 4 dims, incl. $\lambda$ in $s_3$ |
| **F3** ratchet | $s_3$ peer-indexed, not history-indexed |
| **F4** risk transfer | Floor $\alpha$ + HM-optimal $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ |
| **F5**, **F7** cooperation | $s_4$ + $s_5$ directly price the externality (offset the peer-relative sabotage risk of $s_3$) |
| **F6** Goodhart | Multi-dim + subjective override — no single kink to game |
| **A9** selection | Structure attracts cooperative, quality-oriented types ex-ante |

## Implication for the ATE study

Use the composite outcome

$$R_i \;=\; \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\, \mathbf{s}_i \;=\; \beta_3^{*} s_{3}(i) + \beta_4^{*} s_{4}(i) + \beta_5^{*} s_{5} + \beta_6^{*} s_{6}(i)$$

$$\hat\tau \;=\; \bar R_{T=1} - \bar R_{T=0}$$

$\hat\tau$ is (i) invariant to intra-worker task reallocation, (ii) cooperation-aware (via $s_4, s_5$), (iii) noise-optimal (via $\Sigma$-weighting), (iv) filters common shocks (via $s_3$'s peer-relative form).

**Cautions**
- **Peer group definition**: if AI treatment is uneven across peers, $s_3$ contaminates. Fix: define peer group at untreated baseline OR use saturation design.
- **SUTVA / spillovers**: $s_5$ team component embeds treatment spillover — use saturation design to identify direct vs spillover effects.

## Bottom line

Four signals $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$, four weights $(\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)$, plus $\alpha$ and $\lambda$. $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\mathbf{s}_i$ is Quindi's evaluation index AND the outcome variable of the ATE study.

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52 (matrix formula).
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614 (signal-selection theory).
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13, 324–340 (peer benchmark / team component).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240 ($s_6$ subjective term).
- **Chetty, R., Friedman, J. & Rockoff, J. (2014)**. Measuring the impacts of teachers. *AER*, 104(9), 2593–2679 (individual value-added under fixed pay — outcome measurement template).
